stimuli.content: A city transport undertaking runs 300 buses from three depots — North, Central and South — in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
? × 6 − 384 ÷ 16 = 13 × 9 + 3

solution.concept: Simplify each side with ÷ and × before + and −, then isolate the unknown
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 subtracts the 24 from 120 instead of adding it; 20 ignores the 384 ÷ 16 term; 144 stops before dividing by 6.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
∛? ÷ √0.36 = 15

solution.concept: Evaluate the known root, undo the division, then cube
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 is ∛?, not ?; 3,375 = 15³ forgets the √0.36; 216 = 6³ takes √0.36 as 0.4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which of the following fractions lies between 3/7 and 4/9?

solution.concept: Compare by decimals or cross-multiplication; the mediant (a + c)/(b + d) always lies between a/b and c/d
solution.why_others_wrong: 5/11 and 9/20 are slightly larger than 4/9; 2/5 is smaller than 3/7.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 5ˣ = 3, what is the value of 25^(x + 1)?

solution.why_others_wrong: 75 takes 25ˣ as 3 instead of 3²; 34 adds 25 and 9 instead of multiplying; 45 multiplies 9 by 5 instead of 25.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the least number that must be subtracted from 6,412 to make it a perfect square?

solution.concept: Find the largest perfect square not exceeding the number
solution.explanation: 80² = 6,400 and 81² = 6,561, so the largest perfect square below 6,412 is 6,400. Subtract 6,412 − 6,400 = 12.
solution.why_others_wrong: 149 must be added to reach 81² = 6,561; 171 goes one square too far down, to 79² = 6,241; 80 is the square root of 6,400, not the number to subtract.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
0.125 × 0.64 ÷ 0.016 + 1.2 × 0.75 = ?

solution.concept: Work left to right for × and ÷, then add; count decimal places carefully
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.4 takes 0.08 ÷ 0.016 as 0.5; 0.59 misplaces the decimal point in the final sum; 5.09 takes 1.2 × 0.75 as 0.09.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which of the following arranges ∜6, ∛4, √2 and ⁶√10 in descending order?

solution.concept: Bring all the roots to a common index (the LCM of 4, 3, 2 and 6 is 12) and compare the 12th powers
solution.explanation: Raise each number to the 12th power: (∜6)¹² = 6³ = 216, (∛4)¹² = 4⁴ = 256, (√2)¹² = 2⁶ = 64 and (⁶√10)¹² = 10² = 100. So ∛4 > ∜6 > ⁶√10 > √2.
solution.why_others_wrong: ⁶√10 > ∜6 > ∛4 > √2 orders by the number under the root and ignores the index; √2 > ∛4 > ∜6 > ⁶√10 orders by the index alone; ∜6 > ∛4 > ⁶√10 > √2 swaps the top two, which would need 216 > 256.

solution.concept: Split each term: 1/(n(n + 1)(n + 2)) = ½ × [1/(n(n + 1)) − 1/((n + 1)(n + 2))], so the sum telescopes
solution.explanation: Each term is half the difference of two consecutive terms of 1/(n(n + 1)). Adding from n = 2 to n = 8, everything cancels except the first and the last: ½ × [1/(2 × 3) − 1/(9 × 10)] = ½ × (1/6 − 1/90) = ½ × 14/90 = 7/90.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7/45 forgets the factor ½; 1/12 keeps only the first part, ½ × 1/6; 11/144 ends the telescoping at 1/(8 × 9) instead of 1/(9 × 10).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
119.98% of 450.2 − 59.97% of 249.8 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round each percentage and number; 120% of a number is the number plus one-fifth of it
solution.why_others_wrong: 690 adds the two parts instead of subtracting; 375 and 405 are 15 away from the exact value (about 390.3).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
√3249.2 + ∛2743.9 − 6.98 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round to the nearest perfect square and cube: 3249 = 57², 2744 = 14³
solution.why_others_wrong: 71 ignores the − 6.98; 54 and 74 are 10 away from the exact value (about 64.0).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(18.03 × 24.98) ÷ 14.97 + 9.02² ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round to whole numbers; cancel before multiplying
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 doubles 9 instead of squaring it (30 + 18); 121 and 101 are 10 away from the exact value (about 111.4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
4.99³ − 3.01³ ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round the bases first, then cube each one separately
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 cubes the difference, (5 − 3)³; 152 adds the cubes; 16 squares instead of cubing (25 − 9).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(√143.9 + √224.8)² ≈ ?

solution.concept: Find each square root first; the square of a sum is not the sum of the squares
solution.explanation: √143.9 ≈ 12 and √224.8 ≈ 15, so the bracket ≈ 27 and its square ≈ 729.
solution.why_others_wrong: 369 adds 144 and 225 and drops the cross term 2 × 12 × 15; 27 forgets to square; 784 = 28² takes √143.9 as 13.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(65.02% of 1199.8) ÷ (12.98% of 299.7) ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round each percentage and number, evaluate both brackets, then divide
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 and 200 slip a decimal place; 26 takes 12.98% as 10% (780 ÷ 30).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
1/? of 3599.6 ≈ 14.98% of 1999.8

solution.concept: '1/? of N' means N ÷ ?; find the right side first

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
34.97% of (? − 120.3) ≈ 189.04

solution.concept: Divide by the percentage to find the bracket, then undo the subtraction
solution.why_others_wrong: 420 subtracts 120 instead of adding it; 540 is the value of the bracket, not of ?; 750 uses 30% instead of 35% (630 + 120).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
∜624.9 × ∛511.8 + 1/0.2498 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Use 625 = 5⁴ and 512 = 8³; the reciprocal of 0.25 is 4
solution.why_others_wrong: 40.25 adds 0.25 instead of its reciprocal; 204 takes the fourth root of 625 as its square root (25 × 8 + 4); 36 subtracts the 4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
? × 3.01 ≈ √2304.2 × 6.01 + 40.02% of 819.6 − 16.98²

solution.concept: Round every term to a convenient value; finish the right side before dividing by the multiplier of ?
solution.why_others_wrong: 205 forgets to subtract 17²; 194 takes 17² as 34; 119 is 10 away from the exact value (about 109.0).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(√? + 12.01) ÷ 2.998 ≈ 14.99% of 180.2

solution.concept: Work backwards: undo the division, then the addition, then the square root
solution.why_others_wrong: 6561 = 81² forgets to subtract 12; 69 is √?, not ?; 4225 = 65² is far from the exact value (about 4,757).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
?% of ? ≈ 144.02

solution.why_others_wrong: 12 solves ?² = 144 and forgets the ÷ 100; 1200 multiplies by 100 twice; 72 halves 144 as if ?% of ? were 2 × ?.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
12.02% of 24.98% of ? ≈ 31.96 ÷ 3.99 × 5.99

solution.concept: A percentage of a percentage is the product of the two decimals: 12% of 25% = 3%
solution.why_others_wrong: 160 slips a decimal place; 3200 takes 12% of 25% as 1.5%; 1920 takes 12.02% as 10% (48 ÷ 0.025).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
200, 164, 139, 123, 114, ?

solution.concept: The falls are the perfect squares 6², 5², 4², 3², … in decreasing order
solution.why_others_wrong: 113 subtracts 1², skipping 2²; 105 subtracts 9 again; 98 subtracts 16 (4²) again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
13, 17, 25, 32, 37, 47, ?

solution.concept: Each term = previous term + the sum of its digits
solution.why_others_wrong: 57 adds 10 again; 59 adds 12; 52 adds 5, repeating an earlier jump. Only the digit-sum rule fits every step.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
2, 6, 12, 20, ?, 42

solution.concept: Each term is n(n + 1): 1 × 2, 2 × 3, 3 × 4, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 28 adds 8 again; 32 adds 12, skipping 10; 36 = 6² does not lead to 42 by the rule.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
96, 56, ?, 26, 21, 18.5

solution.concept: Each term = previous ÷ 2 + 8
solution.why_others_wrong: 28 only halves 56 and forgets the + 8; 41 assumes equal steps from 56 to 26; 31 extends the last fall of 5 backwards to 26 + 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
8, 20, 50, 125, ?

solution.concept: Each term = previous × 2.5
solution.why_others_wrong: 250 multiplies by 2; 375 multiplies by 3; 437.5 multiplies by 3.5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
6, 15, 33, 69, 141, ?

solution.concept: Each term = previous × 2 + 3
solution.shortcut: The differences 9, 18, 36, 72 double: next difference 144, and 141 + 144 = 285.
solution.why_others_wrong: 282 doubles and forgets the + 3; 288 adds 6 instead of 3; 213 adds 72 again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
3, 10, 21, 36, 55, ?

solution.concept: Each term is n(2n + 1) = 2n² + n; the differences 7, 11, 15, 19 rise by 4
solution.why_others_wrong: 76 adds 21, raising the difference by 2 instead of 4; 74 adds 19 again; 81 = 9² does not fit n(2n + 1).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
5, 7, 12, 22, 39, 65, ?

solution.concept: The differences are n² + 1: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, …
solution.explanation: The differences are 2, 5, 10, 17, 26 = 1² + 1, 2² + 1, 3² + 1, 4² + 1, 5² + 1. The next is 6² + 1 = 37, so the term is 65 + 37 = 102.
solution.why_others_wrong: 101 adds 36 and forgets the + 1; 91 adds 26 again; 100 adds 35, repeating the last rise of 9 in the differences instead of 11.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 2, 8, 48, 384, ?

solution.concept: The multipliers are the even numbers 2, 4, 6, 8, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 3,456 multiplies by 9; 4,608 multiplies by 12; 3,072 multiplies by 8 again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
4, 6, 10, 17, 29, 48, ?

solution.concept: Take differences twice: the second differences are the prime numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, …
solution.explanation: First differences: 2, 4, 7, 12, 19. Second differences: 2, 3, 5, 7 — consecutive primes. The next second difference is 11, so the next first difference is 19 + 11 = 30 and the term is 48 + 30 = 78.
solution.why_others_wrong: 76 takes the second differences as odd numbers (next 9); 74 repeats the second difference 7; 80 skips 11 and uses 13.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 9, 36, 100, 225, ?

solution.concept: Each term is the sum of the first n cubes, which equals the square of the n-th triangular number
solution.explanation: The differences are 8, 27, 64, 125 = 2³, 3³, 4³, 5³, so the next term is 225 + 6³ = 441. Equivalently the terms are 1², 3², 6², 10², 15², and the next triangular number is 21, giving 21² = 441.
solution.why_others_wrong: 361 = 19² continues the square roots 10, 15 by + 4; 450 doubles 225; 400 = 20² continues the roots by + 5 again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
1, 2, 5, 12, ?, 70, 169

solution.concept: Each term = 2 × previous term + the term before that
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 only doubles 12; 36 triples 12; 25 adds 1 to 2 × 12. None of them gives 70 at the next step (2 × 24 + 12 = 60, 2 × 36 + 12 = 84, 2 × 25 + 12 = 62).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
100, 95, 85, 70, 50, 26, −5

solution.concept: The falls are multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30
solution.why_others_wrong: 85, 50 and −5 all fit the rule; −5 looks wrong only if 26 is taken as correct (26 − 30 = −4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
11, 33, 66, 110, 166, 231

solution.concept: The differences are 22, 33, 44, 55, 66: multiples of 11 (the terms are 11 × 1, 11 × 3, 11 × 6, …)
solution.shortcut: Every correct term is a multiple of 11; 166 is not.
solution.why_others_wrong: 66, 110 and 231 are 11 × 6, 11 × 10 and 11 × 21 and fit the pattern.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
5, 40, 10, 34, 20, 28, 41, 22

solution.concept: Two series alternate: odd positions double (5, 10, 20, …) and even positions fall by 6 (40, 34, 28, …)
solution.explanation: Odd positions: 5, 10, 20, then 40 — but the series shows 41. Even positions: 40, 34, 28, 22 fall by 6 and fit. So 41 is wrong.
solution.why_others_wrong: 34, 20 and 22 belong to the two interleaved series and fit their rules.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
2, 3, 5.5, 9.5, 15.5, 22, 30.5

solution.concept: The differences rise by 1.5 each time: 1, 2.5, 4, 5.5, 7, 8.5
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.5, 22 and 30.5 fit once 15.5 is corrected to 15; 22 looks off only if 15.5 is taken as correct.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
3, 6, 18, 36, 106, 216, 648

solution.concept: The multipliers alternate: × 2, × 3, × 2, × 3, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 18, 216 and 648 fit the alternating rule; 216 only looks wrong if 106 is taken as correct.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
1, 3, 5, 11, 21, 42, 85

solution.concept: Each term = previous term + 2 × the term before it (equivalently × 2 + 1 and × 2 − 1 alternately)
solution.why_others_wrong: 11, 21 and 85 fit; 85 confirms 43, since 42 × 2 + 1 = 85 would need the rule to change.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
1, 4, 8, 9, 26, 16, 64, 25

solution.concept: Two series alternate: odd positions are cubes (1³, 2³, 3³, 4³) and even positions are squares (2², 3², 4², 5²)
solution.explanation: Odd positions: 1, 8, ?, 64 = 1³, 2³, …, 4³, so the fifth term should be 3³ = 27, not 26. Even positions: 4, 9, 16, 25 = 2², 3², 4², 5² fit.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9, 16 and 64 are 3², 4² and 4³ and fit their series.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Both quadratics below have only negative roots. Find them and state how x compares with y.
I. x² + 13x + 42 = 0
II. y² + 17y + 72 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: When all coefficients are positive, both roots are negative; compare the smallest x with the largest y
solution.explanation: x = −6 or −7 and y = −8 or −9. The smallest x (−7) is greater than the largest y (−8), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y come from dropping the minus signs (6 and 7 are smaller than 8 and 9).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the roots of the two equations and choose the relation between x and y, if any.
I. x² − 4x − 21 = 0
II. y² − 8y + 15 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: If one x lies above both y values and the other below them, no relation holds for every pair
solution.explanation: x = 7 or −3 and y = 3 or 5. x = 7 is greater than both y values but x = −3 is less than both, so the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y uses only x = 7; x ≤ y and x < y use only x = −3 (or read the root −3 as 3).
solution.final_answer: Option B: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I has no x-term. Find all roots of I and II and pick the relation between x and y that holds for every pair.
I. 4x² − 25 = 0
II. 2y² + 13y + 21 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: x² = k gives two roots ±√k; do not drop the negative one
solution.explanation: I: x² = 25/4, so x = ±2.5. II: (2y + 7)(y + 3) = 0, so y = −3.5 or −3. Even the smaller x (−2.5) is greater than the larger y (−3), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y come from reading the roots of II as +3 and +3.5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve the two equations and mark the relation between x and y.
I. 3x² − 2x − 8 = 0
II. 3y² − 17y + 24 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Split the middle term; then compare the largest x with the smallest y
solution.explanation: I: (3x + 4)(x − 2) = 0, so x = 2 or −4/3. II: (3y − 8)(y − 3) = 0, so y = 8/3 or 3. The largest x (2) is below the smallest y (2.67), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y come from a sign slip in II that gives y = −8/3 and −3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
One equation is linear and the other quadratic. Solve both and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x/4 + x/6 = 5
II. y² − 21y + 108 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Solve the linear equation exactly; a common value makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: I: x/4 + x/6 = 5x/12 = 5, so x = 12. II: (y − 9)(y − 12) = 0, so y = 9 or 12. x = y when y = 12 and x > y when y = 9, so x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y misses y = 12; x < y comes from forgetting to multiply the 5 by 12 when clearing the fractions (3x + 2x = 5 ⇒ x = 1).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations (do not cancel a common factor that could be zero) and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x(x + 3) = 4(x + 3)
II. y² + 2y − 3 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Move everything to one side and factorise; dividing by (x + 3) would lose the root x = −3
solution.explanation: I: x(x + 3) − 4(x + 3) = (x + 3)(x − 4) = 0, so x = −3 or 4. II: (y + 3)(y − 1) = 0, so y = −3 or 1. x = 4 is greater than both y values, but x = −3 is less than y = 1. So the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y come from cancelling (x + 3), which leaves only x = 4; x < y uses only x = −3.
solution.final_answer: Option D: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y that holds for all their roots.
I. 12x² + 7x − 12 = 0
II. 20y² − 31y + 12 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Use the quadratic formula when splitting the middle term is slow; watch for a root common to both equations
solution.explanation: I: discriminant = 49 + 576 = 625, so x = (−7 ± 25)/24 = 3/4 or −4/3. II: discriminant = 961 − 960 = 1, so y = (31 ± 1)/40 = 4/5 or 3/4. x = y = 3/4 is possible and every other pair has x < y, so x ≤ y.
steps: All other pairs x < y ⇒ x ≤ y
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the common root 3/4; x ≥ y holds only for the pair x = y = 3/4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The equations below have irrational coefficients (√2 ≈ 1.414). Solve them and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 3√2x − 8 = 0
II. y² + 5√2y + 12 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Quadratic formula with surds: write the discriminant as a multiple of 2 so that its root is a multiple of √2
solution.explanation: I: discriminant = 18 + 32 = 50, √50 = 5√2, so x = (3√2 ± 5√2)/2 = 4√2 or −√2. II: discriminant = 50 − 48 = 2, so y = (−5√2 ± √2)/2 = −2√2 or −3√2. The smallest x (−√2 ≈ −1.41) is greater than the largest y (−2√2 ≈ −2.83), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y come from taking the roots of II with the wrong sign (2√2 and 3√2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations without cancelling any factor that could be zero, and choose the relation between x and y.
I. (x − 4)² + 3(x − 4) = 0
II. 2y(y − 1) = y − 1

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Take the common bracket out as a factor; each factor can be zero
solution.explanation: I: (x − 4)[(x − 4) + 3] = (x − 4)(x − 1) = 0, so x = 4 or 1. II: 2y(y − 1) − (y − 1) = (y − 1)(2y − 1) = 0, so y = 1 or 1/2. x = 1, y = 1 gives x = y; every other pair has x > y. So x ≥ y.
steps: All other pairs x > y ⇒ x ≥ y
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y comes from cancelling (y − 1), which loses y = 1; x < y comes from writing the factors of I as (x + 4)(x + 1), which gives the negative roots −4 and −1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations (x ≠ 0) and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x/3 + 3/x = 10/3
II. y² − 25y + 156 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Clear the fractions by multiplying by 3x to get a quadratic
solution.explanation: I: multiply by 3x: x² + 9 = 10x, so x² − 10x + 9 = 0 and x = 1 or 9. II: (y − 12)(y − 13) = 0, so y = 12 or 13. The largest x (9) is below the smallest y (12), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y come from a sign slip in II that gives y = −12 and −13; with the correct roots every x is below every y.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 9x² − 30x + 25 = 0
II. 3y² − 11y + 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A perfect-square quadratic has one repeated root
solution.explanation: I: 9x² − 30x + 25 = (3x − 5)² = 0, so x = 5/3 only. II: (3y − 5)(y − 2) = 0, so y = 5/3 or 2. x = y when y = 5/3 and x < y when y = 2, so x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the common value 5/3; x > y comes from taking the roots of II as 5/3 and 2/3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which of the following numbers is divisible by both 4 and 9?

solution.concept: Divisible by 4: the last two digits form a multiple of 4. Divisible by 9: the digit sum is a multiple of 9
solution.explanation: 7,632: 32 is a multiple of 4 and 7 + 6 + 3 + 2 = 18 is a multiple of 9, so it is divisible by both (7,632 = 36 × 212).
steps: 5,418: digit sum 18 ✓ but 18 is not a multiple of 4
7,362: digit sum 18 ✓ but 62 is not a multiple of 4
solution.why_others_wrong: 5,418 and 7,362 pass the test for 9 but fail the test for 4 (7,362 has the same digits as 7,632 in another order); 8,724 passes the test for 4 but its digit sum, 21, is only a multiple of 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A hall floor measuring 9.6 m by 7.2 m is to be paved with identical square tiles, with no tile cut. What is the least number of tiles needed?

solution.concept: The largest square tile that fits exactly has a side equal to the HCF of the two lengths
solution.explanation: In cm the floor is 960 × 720. HCF(960, 720) = 240, so the largest tile is 240 cm × 240 cm. Tiles needed = (960 ÷ 240) × (720 ÷ 240) = 4 × 3 = 12.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 uses 120 cm tiles, a common factor but not the highest; 108 uses 80 cm tiles; 240 is the side of the tile in cm, not the number of tiles.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 17²³ + 23²³ is divided by 40?

solution.concept: For an odd power n, aⁿ + bⁿ is always divisible by a + b
solution.explanation: 23 is odd, so 17²³ + 23²³ is divisible by 17 + 23 = 40. The remainder is 0.
steps: aⁿ + bⁿ is divisible by a + b when n is odd
solution.shortcut: Check: 17²³ leaves 33 and 23²³ leaves 7 on division by 40; 33 + 7 = 40.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33 is the remainder of 17²³ alone; 7 is the remainder of 23²³ alone; 2 treats both powers as leaving remainder 1, a rule that holds only for suitable even powers.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many factors of 2⁴ × 3³ × 5² are perfect squares?

solution.concept: A factor is a perfect square when every prime in it has an even power
solution.explanation: A square factor is 2ᵃ × 3ᵇ × 5ᶜ with a, b and c even: a ∈ {0, 2, 4} (3 ways), b ∈ {0, 2} (2 ways), c ∈ {0, 2} (2 ways). So there are 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 such factors.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 counts all factors, (4 + 1)(3 + 1)(2 + 1); 4 counts the perfect-cube factors; 30 assumes half of all factors are squares.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the largest number that divides 1,305, 4,665 and 6,905 and leaves the same remainder in each case?

solution.concept: If three numbers leave the same remainder on division by d, then d divides every difference; take the HCF of the differences
solution.why_others_wrong: 560 also leaves equal remainders but is not the largest such number; 2,240 is one of the differences but does not divide 3,360; 185 is the common remainder, not the divisor.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 30% of A equals 45% of B, then B is what percentage of A?

solution.concept: Equal parts of A and B: 0.30A = 0.45B, so B/A = 30/45
solution.why_others_wrong: 150% is A as a percentage of B; 33⅓% is how much less B is than A; 15% is the difference between the two percentages.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A laptop bought for ₹60,000 loses 15% of its value in the first year and, in the second year, 10% of its value at the start of that year. What is its value after 2 years?

solution.concept: Successive depreciation multiplies the factors: (1 − 0.15)(1 − 0.10)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹45,000 subtracts 25% of the original price at once; ₹51,000 stops after the first year; ₹43,350 applies 15% in both years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: For positive numbers x, y and z, x% of y is 75 and y% of z is 120. What percentage of x is z?

solution.concept: Write both statements as products: xy/100 = 75 and yz/100 = 120; divide to cancel y
solution.explanation: x% of y = xy/100 = 75 and y% of z = yz/100 = 120. Dividing, z/x = 120/75 = 1.6, so z is 160% of x.
solution.why_others_wrong: 62.5% is x as a percentage of z; 45% reads the difference 120 − 75 as a percentage; 60% is how much more z is than x, written as if it were the whole.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The value of a machine fell from ₹2,50,000 to ₹1,60,000 in 2 years. If it depreciated at the same rate each year (on its value at the start of that year), what was the annual rate of depreciation?

solution.concept: Value after n years = original × (1 − r)ⁿ; take the n-th root of the ratio
solution.why_others_wrong: 18% treats the fall as simple (36% ÷ 2); 36% is the total fall over 2 years; 40% takes the square root of 0.36 (the fall) instead of 0.64 (what remains).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi saves 25% of his income. His income rises by 20%, and he now saves 20% of the new income. By what percentage does his expenditure rise?

solution.concept: Take the old income as 100 and work out both expenditures
solution.explanation: Old: income 100, savings 25, expenditure 75. New: income 120, savings 20% of 120 = 24, expenditure 96. Expenditure rises by 21 on 75, i.e. 28%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% assumes expenditure rises with income; 4% is the fall in savings (25 → 24); 21% reads the rise of 21 on an income of 100 as a percentage of expenditure.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 20% fall in the price of sugar lets a household buy 5 kg more sugar for ₹600. What was the original price per kg?

solution.concept: The money saved on the old quantity buys the extra quantity at the new price
solution.explanation: A 20% fall saves 20% of ₹600 = ₹120, and this buys the extra 5 kg, so the new price is 120 ÷ 5 = ₹24 per kg. The original price was 24 ÷ 0.8 = ₹30 per kg.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹24 is the new price; ₹28.80 adds 20% to ₹24 instead of dividing by 0.8; ₹60 reads the 20% fall as a ₹20 fall per kg.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two numbers are in the ratio 5 : 8 and their difference is 45. What is their sum?

solution.concept: The difference corresponds to 8 − 5 = 3 parts
solution.explanation: 3 parts = 45, so 1 part = 15. The numbers are 75 and 120, and their sum is 13 parts = 195.
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 is the larger number; 75 is the smaller number; 585 multiplies 45 by 13 without first dividing by 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If (x + 3) : (x + 11) = (x − 2) : (x + 2), what is the value of x?

solution.concept: In a proportion a : b = c : d, the product of the extremes equals the product of the means: ad = bc
solution.why_others_wrong: −7/3 multiplies the wrong pairs, (x + 3)(x − 2) = (x + 11)(x + 2); 5.5 drops the constant 6 when expanding; 28 stops at 4x = 28.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The incomes of A, B and C are in the ratio 7 : 9 : 12 and their expenditures are in the ratio 8 : 9 : 15. If A saves one-fourth of his income, what is the ratio of the savings of A, B and C?

solution.concept: Use one unit for incomes and another for expenditures; A's saving links the two units
solution.explanation: Let the incomes be 7k, 9k and 12k. A saves 7k/4, so A spends 21k/4 = 8 parts of expenditure, and one expenditure part = 21k/32. Then B spends 189k/32 and saves 288k/32 − 189k/32 = 99k/32; C spends 315k/32 and saves 384k/32 − 315k/32 = 69k/32; A saves 56k/32. Ratio 56 : 99 : 69.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 : 9 : 12 assumes everyone saves a quarter; 8 : 9 : 15 is the expenditure ratio; 69 : 99 : 56 lists the savings in reverse order.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The price of a diamond varies directly as the square of its weight. A diamond worth ₹1,44,000 breaks into three pieces whose weights are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. What is the loss caused by the breakage?

solution.concept: Price ∝ weight², so compare the sum of the squares of the parts with the square of the whole
solution.explanation: Whole weight = 6 parts, so its price corresponds to 6² = 36 units: 1 unit = ₹4,000. The pieces are worth 1², 2² and 3² units = 14 units = ₹56,000. Loss = 1,44,000 − 56,000 = ₹88,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹56,000 is the value of the pieces, not the loss; ₹1,08,000 subtracts only the largest piece; ₹1,20,000 adds the weights (6) instead of their squares (14).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bag contains ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 coins whose total VALUES are in the ratio 5 : 4 : 2. The total value of the coins is ₹1,100. How many coins are there in the bag?

solution.concept: Split the value first, then divide each share by its coin's denomination
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,100 treats each rupee as one coin; 680 divides the ₹400 by 5 and the ₹200 by 2 (wrong coins); 540 leaves out the ₹2 coins.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A mother's present age is 3 years more than three times her daughter's present age. Three years from now, the mother's age will be 10 years more than twice the daughter's age then. What is the mother's present age?

solution.concept: Write both statements as equations in the daughter's present age
solution.explanation: Let the daughter be d. Mother = 3d + 3. In 3 years: 3d + 6 = 2(d + 3) + 10 = 2d + 16, so d = 10 and the mother is 3 × 10 + 3 = 33.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 years is the daughter's age; 36 years is the mother's age three years from now; 30 years forgets the '3 more than' (3 × 10).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of A and B are in the ratio 6 : 5 and add up to 44 years. After how many years will their ages be in the ratio 8 : 7?

solution.concept: Find the present ages from the sum, then add the same n to both
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 years subtracts the ratio terms (8 − 6); 4 years is the age gap; 12 years gives 36 : 32 = 9 : 8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A father is now three times as old as the sum of the ages of his two sons. Twenty years from now, his age will equal the sum of their ages. What is the father's present age?

solution.concept: In 20 years the father gains 20 years, but the two sons together gain 40
solution.explanation: Let the sons' total now be S, so the father is 3S. In 20 years: 3S + 20 = S + 40, so 2S = 20, S = 10 and the father is 30.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 years is the father's age 20 years from now; 10 years is the sons' present total; 60 years forgets to add 20 years to the father's own age (3S = S + 40).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A father's age, a two-digit number, has the same digits as his son's age in reverse order. One year ago the father was exactly twice as old as the son. What is the father's present age?

solution.concept: Write the ages as 10a + b and 10b + a and look for digit solutions
solution.explanation: Let the father be 10a + b and the son 10b + a. Then 10a + b − 1 = 2(10b + a − 1), so 8a = 19b − 1. The only digits that work are b = 3, a = 7. The father is 73 and the son 37 (a year ago: 72 = 2 × 36).
solution.why_others_wrong: 37 years is the son's age; 72 years is the father's age one year ago; 74 years is his age a year from now.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the average of all the multiples of 7 between 50 and 150?

solution.concept: Equally spaced numbers: average = (first + last) ÷ 2
solution.explanation: The multiples of 7 between 50 and 150 run from 56 to 147. Their average is (56 + 147) ÷ 2 = 101.5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 averages 50 and 150, which are not multiples of 7; 98 = 7 × 14 is a middle multiple, not the average; 105 starts from 63 and skips 56.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In an examination, 60% of the candidates were boys. The boys' average score was 54 and the average score of all the candidates was 57.6. What was the girls' average score?

solution.concept: Overall average = weighted average: 0.6 × boys' average + 0.4 × girls' average
solution.why_others_wrong: 61.2 treats boys and girls as equal in number; 60 swaps the shares (40% boys); 66.6 adds the gap 3.6 ÷ 0.4 = 9 to the overall average instead of to the boys' average.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A batsman's average was 36 runs per innings after a certain number of innings. He then scored 96 in the next innings, which raised his average to 39. How many runs must he score in the following innings to raise his average to 40?

solution.concept: First find the number of innings from the change in average; then the runs needed = new total − old total
solution.explanation: If he had played n innings: 36n + 96 = 39(n + 1), so 3n = 57 and n = 19. After 20 innings his total is 20 × 39 = 780. For an average of 40 over 21 innings he needs 840, i.e. 840 − 780 = 60 runs.
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 uses the old average 36 for 20 innings; 59 counts one innings too few (40 × 20 − 39 × 19); 99 simply adds 3 to the last score.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The cost price and the selling price of an article are in the ratio 5 : 6. What is the profit percentage?

solution.concept: Profit % = (SP − CP) ÷ CP × 100
solution.explanation: Take CP = 5 and SP = 6. Profit = 1, which is 1/5 = 20% of the cost price.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16⅔% divides the profit by the selling price; 120% is SP as a percentage of CP; 83⅓% is CP as a percentage of SP.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If the selling price of an article is doubled, the profit becomes three times as large. What is the profit percentage at the original selling price?

solution.concept: Write both profits in terms of CP and SP: 2SP − CP = 3(SP − CP)
solution.explanation: 2SP − CP = 3SP − 3CP gives SP = 2CP. So the profit equals the cost price: a profit of 100%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 300% is the profit percentage at the doubled price (4CP − CP = 3CP); 200% is the rise in the profit itself (from P to 3P); 50% is the profit as a percentage of the selling price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By selling 45 lemons for ₹40, a vendor loses 20%. How many lemons should he sell for ₹24 to gain 20%?

solution.concept: Find the cost of the 45 lemons from the loss, then the selling price that gives the required gain
solution.explanation: ₹40 is 80% of the cost, so 45 lemons cost ₹50. For a 20% gain they must sell for ₹60, i.e. 45 lemons for ₹60. For ₹24 he should give 45 × 24 ÷ 60 = 18 lemons.
solution.why_others_wrong: 27 keeps the old rate of 45 lemons for ₹40; 22.5 applies the 20% gain to ₹40 instead of to the cost; 13.5 doubles ₹40 to ₹80 for the 45 lemons.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By selling an article at three-fourths of its marked price, a shopkeeper incurs a loss of 10%. What would his profit percentage be if he sold it at the marked price?

solution.concept: Link the marked price to the cost price: 0.75 × MP = 0.90 × CP
solution.explanation: 0.75 MP = 0.9 CP, so MP = 1.2 CP. Selling at the marked price gives a profit of 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15% subtracts the 10% loss from the 25% cut; 35% adds the 25% cut and the 10% loss; 25% takes the cut of one-fourth as the markup.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A dealer bought a television and a refrigerator for ₹82,000 in all. He sold the television at a profit of 25% and the refrigerator at a loss of 20%, and both fetched the same price. What did the television cost him?

solution.concept: Equal selling prices: 1.25 × CP(TV) = 0.80 × CP(fridge); split ₹82,000 in that ratio
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹50,000 is the refrigerator's cost; ₹41,000 splits the total equally; ₹40,000 is the common selling price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper marks his goods 40% above cost. He sells half his stock at the marked price, one-fourth at a discount of 20% and the rest at a discount of 40%. What is his overall profit percentage?

solution.concept: Find the revenue from each part of the stock per unit of cost, then add
solution.explanation: Take the cost of the whole stock as 100, so it is marked at 140. Half at MP: 70. One-fourth at 20% off: 35 × 0.8 = 28. One-fourth at 40% off: 35 × 0.6 = 21. Revenue = 119, a profit of 19%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12% averages the three discounts as 20% without weighting by stock; 25% subtracts the weighted discount (15) from the markup (40); 40% ignores the discounts.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A grocer buys 60 kg of rice at ₹40 per kg and 40 kg at ₹50 per kg and mixes them. In handling, 4% of the mixture by weight is lost. At what price per kg must he sell the rest to gain 20% on his total outlay?

solution.concept: Required revenue = total cost × 1.2; divide it by the quantity actually left to sell
solution.explanation: Cost = 60 × 40 + 40 × 50 = ₹4,400. For a 20% gain he needs ₹5,280. Only 96 kg remain, so the price must be 5,280 ÷ 96 = ₹55 per kg.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹52.80 ignores the 4% loss (divides by 100 kg); ₹45.83 recovers only the cost (4,400 ÷ 96); ₹54 averages ₹40 and ₹50 without weighting and ignores the loss.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shop offers 'Buy 2, get 1 free' on soaps of the same price. What single discount percentage is this equivalent to?

solution.concept: Discount % = value given free ÷ value of everything taken × 100
solution.explanation: The customer takes 3 soaps and pays for 2. The free soap is 1 of 3, so the discount is 1/3 = 33⅓%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50% compares the free soap with the 2 paid for; 25% treats it as 1 free out of 4; 66⅔% is the fraction actually paid.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper allows a discount of 10% on the marked price, and the discount in rupees is exactly equal to his profit in rupees. By what percentage is the marked price above the cost price?

solution.concept: Take MP = 100; then the discount is 10 and the profit is also 10
solution.explanation: MP = 100, discount = 10, so SP = 90. Profit = 10, so CP = 90 − 10 = 80. The marked price is 20 above the cost, which is 20/80 = 25% above it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% measures the markup on the marked price; 12.5% is the profit percentage (10/80); 10% repeats the discount.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A store gives 20% off the marked price, then a further 10% off the discounted price on bills above ₹5,000, and finally a 5% cashback on the amount paid. What is the net cost to a customer who buys a single item marked ₹7,500?

solution.concept: Apply each reduction to the amount left after the previous one; check the ₹5,000 condition on the discounted bill
solution.explanation: After 20% off: ₹6,000, which is above ₹5,000, so a further 10% off gives ₹5,400. A 5% cashback on ₹5,400 is ₹270, so the net cost is ₹5,130.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹4,875 adds the three rates and takes 35% off the marked price; ₹5,400 forgets the cashback; ₹5,025 takes the cashback on the marked price (₹375) instead of on the amount paid.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum of money amounts to ₹7,260 in 4 years at 5% per annum simple interest. What is the sum?

solution.concept: Amount = P(1 + rt/100), so P = Amount ÷ (1 + rt/100)
solution.explanation: In 4 years at 5% the interest is 20% of P, so 1.2P = 7,260 and P = ₹6,050.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹5,808 takes 20% off the amount instead of dividing by 1.2; ₹1,210 is the interest; ₹6,600 uses only 10% (2 years).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many years will ₹3,600 earn at 5% per annum simple interest the same interest that ₹4,500 earns in 4 years at 6% per annum?

solution.concept: Find the target interest first, then solve SI = Prt/100 for t
solution.explanation: ₹4,500 at 6% for 4 years earns 4,500 × 6 × 4 ÷ 100 = ₹1,080. ₹3,600 at 5% earns ₹180 a year, so it needs 1,080 ÷ 180 = 6 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 years uses 6% for the second sum as well; 4.8 years ignores the different principals (4 × 6/5); 3.84 years inverts the ratio of the principals.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹6,500 is divided into two parts. The simple interest on the first part at 5% per annum for 6 years equals the simple interest on the second part at 4% per annum for 5 years. What is the first part?

solution.concept: Equal interest: P₁ × 30% = P₂ × 20%, so P₁ : P₂ = 20 : 30 = 2 : 3
solution.explanation: The first part earns 30% of itself and the second 20% of itself. For equal interest, P₁ : P₂ = 2 : 3, so the first part is 2/5 × 6,500 = ₹2,600.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,900 is the second part (or takes the ratio as 3 : 2); ₹3,250 splits the sum equally; ₹1,300 is the difference between the two parts.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Neha deposits ₹40,000 at 7% per annum simple interest. After 2 years she adds ₹20,000 to the same deposit at the same rate. What total interest will she have earned at the end of 5 years from the first deposit?

solution.concept: Split the time: the principal is ₹40,000 for the first 2 years and ₹60,000 for the next 3
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹21,000 charges the full ₹60,000 for all 5 years; ₹14,000 ignores the second deposit; ₹16,800 swaps the periods (₹60,000 for 2 years, ₹40,000 for 3).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The simple interest on a sum for 4 years is ₹1,440. If the rate were 1% higher and the time 1 year longer, the simple interest would be ₹2,000. What is the sum?

solution.concept: Write both interests as P × r × t/100 and eliminate the product Pr
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹11,200 credits the whole ₹560 increase to the extra 1% over 5 years; ₹14,000 keeps the time at 4 years in the second case; ₹3,600 assumes a 10% rate (1,440 ÷ 0.4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the compound interest on ₹25,000 for 2 years at 12% per annum, compounded annually?

solution.why_others_wrong: ₹6,000 is the simple interest; ₹3,000 is one year's interest; ₹31,360 is the amount, not the interest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the effective annual rate of interest on a deposit that pays 8% per annum compounded quarterly (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Effective rate = (1 + r/4)⁴ − 1 for quarterly compounding
solution.explanation: Each quarter pays 2%. Over a year, 1.02⁴ = 1.0824 (to four decimals), so the effective annual rate is 8.24%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8% ignores compounding; 8.16% compounds only half-yearly (1.04² − 1); 36.05% applies the full 8% every quarter.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In what time will ₹8,000 amount to ₹9,261 at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded half-yearly?

solution.concept: Half-yearly: rate 5% per half-year; solve 1.05ⁿ = 9,261/8,000 for the number of half-years
solution.explanation: 9,261/8,000 = (21/20)³ = 1.05³. So the money is compounded for 3 half-years, i.e. 1½ years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 years counts half-years as years; 1 year gives only ₹8,820; 2 years would give more than ₹9,261 (₹9,724.05).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The compound interest (compounded annually) on a sum is ₹1,320 for the second year and ₹1,452 for the third year. What is the sum?

solution.concept: Interest of a year = previous year's interest × (1 + r); the second year's interest is P × (1 + r) × r
solution.explanation: 1,452 ÷ 1,320 = 1.1, so the rate is 10%. Second-year interest = P × 1.1 × 0.1 = 0.11P = 1,320, so P = ₹12,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹13,200 treats ₹1,320 as the first year's interest; ₹14,520 treats ₹1,452 as the first year's interest; ₹11,000 divides 13,200 by 1.2 instead of 1.1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ramesh invests ₹37,000 in two parts: one at 10% per annum compound interest (compounded annually) and the other at 8% per annum simple interest. After 2 years the two parts have earned equal interest. How much did he invest at compound interest?

solution.concept: Two-year CI at 10% = 21% of the principal; two-year SI at 8% = 16%
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹21,000 is the part at simple interest; ₹18,500 splits the money equally; ₹16,444.44 treats the 10% part as simple interest too (0.20x = 0.16y).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: At what rate per annum, compounded annually, will ₹15,625 amount to ₹17,576 in 3 years?

solution.concept: (1 + r)³ = A/P; recognise 15,625 = 25³ and 17,576 = 26³
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.16% treats the growth as simple interest (12.49% ÷ 3); 12.49% is the total growth over 3 years; 6.06% takes the square root instead of the cube root.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B invest ₹40,000 and ₹50,000 in a business for the same period. The business makes a loss of ₹9,000, shared in the ratio of their investments. What is A's share of the loss?

solution.concept: Losses, like profits, are shared in the ratio of capital × time
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹5,000 is B's share; ₹4,500 splits the loss equally; ₹3,600 takes A's share as 40% of the loss.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A invests ₹30,000 for 12 months and B invests some money for 10 months. Their profits are in the ratio 2 : 3. How much did B invest?

solution.concept: Profit ratio = ratio of capital × months
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹45,000 ignores the different periods; ₹37,500 swaps the periods (multiplies by 10/12 instead of 12/10); ₹24,000 uses the profit ratio upside down.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C invest ₹20,000, ₹30,000 and ₹50,000 in a business. They agree that one-third of the profit is shared equally and the rest in the ratio of their investments. Out of a profit of ₹90,000, how much more does C get than A?

solution.concept: The equal part adds the same amount to everyone, so only the capital-based part creates a difference
solution.explanation: Equal part: ₹30,000, i.e. ₹10,000 each. Capital part: ₹60,000 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5, i.e. ₹12,000, ₹18,000, ₹30,000. A gets ₹22,000 and C gets ₹40,000; the difference is ₹18,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹27,000 shares the whole profit by capital; ₹40,000 is C's share; ₹22,000 is A's share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C start a business with capitals in the ratio ½ : ⅓ : ¼. After 4 months A increases his capital by 50%. Out of a profit of ₹1,95,000 at the end of the year, what is B's share?

solution.concept: Convert the fractional ratio to whole numbers (× 12), then multiply each capital by its time
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹60,000 ignores A's increase (6 : 4 : 3); ₹65,000 reads the ratio from the denominators as 2 : 3 : 4; ₹1,04,000 is A's share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B start a business with ₹60,000 and ₹40,000. After 4 months, A withdraws an amount x and B adds the same amount x to his capital. At the end of the year the profit is shared equally. What is x?

solution.concept: Equal profit shares need equal capital-months over the whole year
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹10,000 only equalises the two capitals for the last 8 months and ignores A's lead in the first 4; ₹20,000 treats the change as happening after 6 months; ₹30,000 forgets that B also adds x.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 60-litre sugar solution contains 20% sugar. If 20 litres of water are added, what is the percentage of sugar in the new solution?

solution.concept: Adding water does not change the amount of sugar; only the total volume grows
solution.explanation: Sugar = 20% of 60 = 12 litres. New volume = 80 litres. Sugar % = 12 ÷ 80 = 15%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% ignores the added water; 12% divides 12 litres by 100 instead of 80; 25% takes the 20 litres added as sugar.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Jug P contains milk and water in the ratio 2 : 1 and jug Q contains them in the ratio 1 : 3. In what ratio must the contents of P and Q be mixed to get a mixture with equal amounts of milk and water?

solution.concept: Apply alligation to the fraction of milk in each jug: P has 2/3, Q has 1/4, target 1/2
solution.explanation: P : Q = (1/2 − 1/4) : (2/3 − 1/2) = 1/4 : 1/6 = 3 : 2. Check: 3 parts of P give 2 of milk, 2 parts of Q give 1/2 of milk; 2.5 out of 5 is half.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 3 applies alligation to the ratios 2 and 1/3 themselves instead of the milk fractions; 1 : 1 uses P's water fraction (1/3) in place of its milk fraction; 8 : 3 is just the ratio of the two milk fractions.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A fuel depot has 300 litres of E10 petrol (10% ethanol by volume). How many litres of a 70% ethanol blend must be added to make E20 petrol (20% ethanol)?

solution.explanation: E10 and the 70% blend must be mixed in the ratio 5 : 1, so 300 litres of E10 need 300 ÷ 5 = 60 litres of the blend. Check: (30 + 42) ÷ 360 = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,500 litres inverts the alligation ratio; 42.86 litres forgets that the added blend also increases the total volume (it solves 30 + 0.7x = 60); 30 litres simply takes 10% of 300.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 50-litre tank holds a juice mixture that is 40% concentrate. 10 litres are drawn off and replaced with water. Then 10 litres of the new mixture are drawn off and replaced with pure concentrate. What percentage of the final mixture is concentrate?

solution.concept: Track the litres of concentrate step by step; each draw removes the current percentage
solution.explanation: Start: 20 L of concentrate. Draw 10 L (40%): 16 L left; add water: 16 L in 50 L = 32%. Draw 10 L (32%): 16 − 3.2 = 12.8 L; add 10 L concentrate: 22.8 L in 50 L = 45.6%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40% assumes the two steps cancel; 52% forgets that the second draw also removes concentrate; 44% removes concentrate at the original 40% strength in the second draw.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A grocer has 20 kg of rice at ₹30 per kg and 30 kg of rice at ₹40 per kg. How many kg of rice at ₹55 per kg must he mix with them so that the whole mixture is worth ₹45 per kg?

solution.concept: Total value = total quantity × mean price; the two cheaper lots can first be combined into one
solution.explanation: The 50 kg already held cost 600 + 1,200 = ₹1,800, i.e. ₹36 per kg. Alligation of ₹36 and ₹55 about ₹45: cheap : dear = 10 : 9, so the ₹55 rice = 50 × 9/10 = 45 kg. Check: 1,800 + 45 × 55 = 4,275 = 95 × 45.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 kg averages ₹30 and ₹40 as ₹35 without weighting; 15 kg balances only the ₹40 rice; 30 kg balances only the ₹30 rice.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A milkman buys milk at ₹48 per litre, adds water and sells the mixture at ₹54 per litre, making a profit of 35%. In what ratio did he mix water with milk?

solution.concept: Find the cost price of the mixture from the selling price and the profit; water costs nothing
solution.explanation: Cost of 1 litre of mixture = 54 ÷ 1.35 = ₹40. Milk costs ₹48, so each litre of mixture contains 40/48 = 5/6 litre of milk and 1/6 litre of water. Water : milk = 1 : 5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 : 1 is milk to water; 1 : 6 is water to the whole mixture; 1 : 8 ignores the profit and compares the extra ₹6 with ₹48.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B together can finish a piece of work in 10 days, and A alone can finish it in 15 days. In how many days can B alone finish it?

solution.concept: B's one-day work = (A + B)'s one-day work − A's one-day work
solution.explanation: Together they do 1/10 of the work a day and A does 1/15, so B does 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30 a day and needs 30 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 days subtracts the day counts (15 − 10); 25 days adds them; 6 days adds the two rates as if both were individual workers (10 × 15 ÷ 25).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 12 men can complete a job in 10 days. They start together, but after 4 days 3 of them leave. In how many days in all is the job completed?

solution.concept: Count the work in man-days: total = 12 × 10 = 120
solution.explanation: In the first 4 days 12 men do 48 man-days of work, leaving 72. The remaining 9 men need 72 ÷ 9 = 8 more days, so the job takes 4 + 8 = 12 days in all.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 days is only the time after the 3 men leave; 13⅓ days assumes 9 men worked from the start (120 ÷ 9); 10 days is the original plan.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A can finish a job in 12 days and is paid ₹600 a day; B can finish it in 18 days and is paid ₹450 a day. Payment is only for the days worked. What is the least total wage at which the job can be finished — by A alone, B alone or both together?

solution.concept: Compare the total cost of each option: days needed × daily wage
solution.explanation: A alone: 12 × 600 = ₹7,200. B alone: 18 × 450 = ₹8,100. Together they need 1 ÷ (1/12 + 1/18) = 7.2 days at ₹1,050 a day = ₹7,560. The least is ₹7,200 (A alone).
solution.shortcut: A's cost per whole job (₹7,200) is lower than B's (₹8,100), so any share of B's work only adds cost.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹7,560 is the cost of both working together; ₹8,100 is B alone; ₹7,650 averages the two single costs.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A man works twice as fast as a woman, and a woman works twice as fast as a child. 2 men, 3 women and 4 children together finish a job in 6 days. How long will 1 man, 1 woman and 1 child take to finish it together?

solution.concept: Convert everyone to child-units: man = 4, woman = 2, child = 1
solution.explanation: The group does 2 × 4 + 3 × 2 + 4 × 1 = 18 units a day, so the job is 18 × 6 = 108 units. One man, one woman and one child do 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 units a day and need 108 ÷ 7 = 15 3/7 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 days counts heads (9 people against 3) and ignores efficiency; 16.8 days takes a man as equal to a woman (both 2 units); 12 days divides 108 by the 9 people of the group.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A takes 6 days less than B to finish a job alone. Working together, they finish it in 4 days. How many days does A alone take?

solution.concept: Let A take a days and B take a + 6 days; their one-day works add to 1/4
solution.explanation: 1/a + 1/(a + 6) = 1/4 gives 4(2a + 6) = a(a + 6), i.e. a² − 2a − 24 = 0, so (a − 6)(a + 4) = 0 and a = 6 (a number of days cannot be negative). B takes 12 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 days is B's time; 8 days assumes A and B are equally fast (2 × 4); 10 days adds the 6-day gap to the joint time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A contractor plans to finish a road in 40 days with 30 workers working 8 hours a day. After 20 days only 3/8 of the road is complete. From then on everyone works 10 hours a day. How many more workers must he employ to finish on time? (All workers work at the same rate.)

solution.concept: Measure the work in man-hours from what was actually achieved, not from the plan
solution.explanation: In 20 days, 30 × 20 × 8 = 4,800 man-hours produced 3/8 of the road, so the whole road needs 12,800 man-hours and 8,000 remain. The remaining 20 days at 10 hours give 200 hours, so 8,000 ÷ 200 = 40 workers are needed: 10 more.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 keeps the 8-hour day (8,000 ÷ 160 = 50 workers); 40 is the total number of workers needed, not the extra; 0 trusts the original plan of 9,600 man-hours instead of the actual progress.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two pipes together fill a tank in 6 hours. One of them alone fills it in 10 hours. How long does the other pipe alone take to fill it?

solution.concept: Rate of the second pipe = joint rate − rate of the first
solution.explanation: Together the pipes fill 1/6 of the tank an hour and the first fills 1/10, so the second fills 1/6 − 1/10 = 1/15 an hour and needs 15 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 hours subtracts the times; 16 hours adds them; 3.75 hours adds the two rates (the time if the 6-hour and 10-hour figures were two separate pipes).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours and pipe B in 18 hours. A is opened on the empty tank, and 3 hours later B is also opened. How long does it take in all to fill the tank?

solution.concept: Work out the part filled by A alone, then the time for both pipes to fill the rest
solution.explanation: In 3 hours A fills 3/12 = 1/4. Together A and B fill 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 an hour, so the remaining 3/4 takes 3/4 ÷ 5/36 = 5.4 hours. Total = 3 + 5.4 = 8.4 hours = 8 hours 24 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 hours 12 minutes assumes both pipes ran from the start; 5 hours 24 minutes is only the time after B is opened; 8 hours 40 minutes reads 0.4 hour as 40 minutes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The rate at which water flows through a pipe is proportional to the area of its circular cross-section (assume the same water speed). A pipe of diameter 2 cm fills a tank in 36 minutes. How long will a pipe of diameter 3 cm take to fill the same tank?

solution.concept: Cross-section area ∝ diameter², and time ∝ 1 ÷ rate
solution.explanation: The area grows by (3/2)² = 9/4, so the flow rate is 9/4 times as fast and the time is 36 × 4/9 = 16 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 minutes takes the rate as proportional to the diameter; 54 minutes multiplies by 3/2 as if a wider pipe were slower; 10⅔ minutes uses the cube of the diameter ratio.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours and pipe B empties the full tank in 9 hours. Starting with the tank empty, A and B are opened alternately for one hour each, beginning with A. After how many hours will the tank first be full?

solution.concept: Each 2-hour cycle adds 1/6 − 1/9 = 1/18; stop as soon as A's hour can top the tank up
solution.explanation: Each A–B cycle adds 1/18. The tank is full when A's hour starts with at least 1 − 1/6 = 5/6 in it. After 15 cycles (30 hours) the tank holds 15/18 = 5/6, and in the 31st hour A adds 1/6. So it is full after 31 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 hours keeps both pipes open together all the time; 36 hours forgets that the tank fills during A's hour, before B can empty it; 30 hours stops when the tank is only 5/6 full.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cyclist covers 12 km in 40 minutes and the next 18 km in 50 minutes. What is the average speed for the whole ride?

solution.concept: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time
solution.explanation: Total distance = 30 km and total time = 90 minutes = 1.5 hours, so the average speed = 30 ÷ 1.5 = 20 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 19.8 km/h averages the two section speeds (18 and 21.6 km/h) instead of using total distance ÷ total time; 18 km/h and 21.6 km/h are the speeds of the two sections alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Excluding stoppages, a bus runs at 54 km/h; including stoppages, its average speed is 45 km/h. For how many minutes does the bus stop per hour?

solution.concept: In each hour the bus loses 54 − 45 = 9 km; find the time it would need to run those 9 km
solution.explanation: Because of stoppages the bus covers 9 km less per hour. At 54 km/h, 9 km takes 9/54 hour = 10 minutes, so it stops 10 minutes per hour.
steps: Time for 9 km at 54 km/h = 9/54 h
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 minutes reads the 9 km as minutes; 12 minutes divides 9 by 45 instead of 54; 50 minutes is the running time per hour.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two cars start at the same time from towns X and Y and drive towards each other at 50 km/h and 40 km/h. When they meet, the faster car has travelled 30 km more than the slower one. How far apart are X and Y?

solution.concept: The faster car gains 50 − 40 = 10 km every hour, which tells you the travel time
solution.explanation: The gap between their distances grows by 10 km each hour, so a 30 km gap means they met after 3 hours. In 3 hours they cover (50 + 40) × 3 = 270 km together, which is the distance XY.
solution.why_others_wrong: 150 km is only the faster car's distance; 120 km is only the slower car's; 90 km is one hour of travel.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B start at the same time from towns P and Q and walk towards each other at constant speeds. They first meet 12 km from P. Each continues to the other town, turns back at once, and they meet again 8 km from Q. What is the distance between P and Q?

solution.concept: By the second meeting the two together have covered three times the distance PQ, so each has walked three times his distance to the first meeting
solution.explanation: At the first meeting they have together covered PQ, and A has walked 12 km. By the second meeting they have together covered 3 × PQ, so A has walked 3 × 12 = 36 km. A has gone from P to Q and come back 8 km, i.e. PQ + 8 = 36, so PQ = 28 km.
steps: First meeting: total = PQ, A = 12 km
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 km adds 12 and 8; 36 km is the distance A walks before the second meeting; 44 km adds 8 instead of subtracting it (36 + 8).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Walking at 5 km/h, a man reaches his office 6 minutes late; walking at 6 km/h, he reaches 4 minutes early. At what speed should he walk to reach exactly on time?

solution.concept: The two times differ by 10 minutes; find the distance, then the exact time available
solution.explanation: d/5 − d/6 = 10/60 gives d/30 = 1/6, so d = 5 km. At 5 km/h he takes 1 hour, which is 6 minutes late, so the time available is 54 minutes = 0.9 hour. Required speed = 5 ÷ 0.9 = 50/9 = 5 5/9 km/h.
steps: Time at 5 km/h = 60 min (6 min late)
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.5 km/h averages the two speeds; 5 5/11 km/h is their harmonic mean (equal distances), which does not fit these times; 4 6/11 km/h adds the 6 minutes instead of subtracting them (5 ÷ 1.1).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat covers 32 km downstream in 2 hours and 24 km upstream in 3 hours. What is its speed in still water?

solution.concept: Boat speed = (downstream speed + upstream speed) ÷ 2
solution.explanation: Downstream speed = 32 ÷ 2 = 16 km/h; upstream speed = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 km/h. Boat speed = (16 + 8) ÷ 2 = 12 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 km/h is the speed of the stream; 24 km/h adds the two speeds and forgets to halve; 8 km/h is the upstream speed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A man can row at 6 km/h in still water. When the stream flows at 1.2 km/h, it takes him 1 hour to row to a place and come back. How far is the place?

solution.concept: Time downstream + time upstream = 1 hour, with speeds 7.2 and 4.8 km/h
solution.shortcut: Distance = (u × v) ÷ (u + v) × total time = 34.56 ÷ 12 = 2.88 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 km ignores the stream (half an hour each way at 6 km/h); 3.6 km uses the downstream speed for half an hour; 2.4 km uses the upstream speed for half an hour.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat goes from A to B downstream in 4 hours and returns from B to A in 6 hours. How long would a log take to float from A to B with the stream?

solution.concept: Stream speed = (downstream speed − upstream speed) ÷ 2; a log moves at the stream's speed
solution.explanation: Let AB = d. Downstream speed = d/4 and upstream speed = d/6, so the stream speed = (d/4 − d/6) ÷ 2 = d/24. The log takes d ÷ (d/24) = 24 hours.
solution.shortcut: Take AB = 24 km: downstream 6 km/h, upstream 4 km/h, stream 1 km/h, log 24 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 hours forgets to halve the difference of the speeds; 10 hours adds the two times; 4.8 hours is the harmonic mean of 4 and 6, which has nothing to do with the stream.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 360 m long train running at 72 km/h passes a 140 m long goods train standing on a parallel track. How long does it take to pass the goods train completely?

solution.concept: A standing train is like a platform: distance = sum of the two lengths
solution.explanation: 72 km/h = 20 m/s. Distance = 360 + 140 = 500 m. Time = 500 ÷ 20 = 25 seconds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 seconds counts only the moving train's length; 7 seconds counts only the goods train's length; 6.94 seconds divides 500 m by 72 without converting km/h to m/s.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two trains of equal length take 10 seconds and 15 seconds respectively to pass a telegraph post. If they run in opposite directions on parallel tracks, how long will they take to cross each other completely?

solution.concept: Let each length be L: speeds are L/10 and L/15; crossing distance = 2L at the sum of the speeds
solution.explanation: Time = 2L ÷ (L/10 + L/15) = 2L ÷ (L/6) = 12 seconds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12.5 seconds averages the two times; 25 seconds adds them; 6 seconds forgets that the distance is both lengths (L ÷ L/6).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A fast train running at 72 km/h overtakes a slow train running at 36 km/h on a parallel track in the same direction. It passes the slow train completely in 30 seconds, and a passenger sitting in the slow train sees the fast train go past him in 18 seconds. What is the length of the slow train?

solution.concept: Relative speed (same direction) = 72 − 36 = 36 km/h = 10 m/s; the passenger is a point, so 18 s gives the fast train's length alone
solution.explanation: Relative speed = 10 m/s. Passing the passenger: fast train's length = 10 × 18 = 180 m. Passing the whole slow train: both lengths = 10 × 30 = 300 m. So the slow train is 300 − 180 = 120 m long.
solution.why_others_wrong: 180 m is the fast train's length; 300 m is the two lengths together; 360 m adds the speeds although the trains move the same way (30 m/s × 12 s).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The parallel sides of a trapezium are 18 cm and 12 cm, and the distance between them is 8 cm. What is its area?

solution.concept: Area of a trapezium = ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × height
solution.why_others_wrong: 240 cm² forgets the ½; 144 cm² uses only the longer side (18 × 8); 96 cm² uses only the shorter side (12 × 8).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the perimeter of a semicircular plate of radius 14 cm? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Perimeter of a semicircle = half the circumference + the diameter = πr + 2r
solution.explanation: πr = 22/7 × 14 = 44 cm, and the straight edge is the diameter, 28 cm. Perimeter = 44 + 28 = 72 cm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 44 cm leaves out the straight edge; 88 cm is the full circle's circumference; 58 cm adds the radius instead of the diameter.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the area of a sector of a circle of radius 21 cm whose central angle is 120°? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Sector area = (θ/360°) × πr²
solution.explanation: πr² = 22/7 × 441 = 1,386 cm². A 120° sector is one-third of the circle: 1,386 ÷ 3 = 462 cm².
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,386 cm² is the whole circle; 44 cm is the arc length, not an area; 231 cm² uses 60° instead of 120°.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The curved surface area of a right circular cylinder is 1,320 cm² and its height is 15 cm. What is its volume? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Find the radius from CSA = 2πrh, then use V = πr²h
solution.why_others_wrong: 3,080 cm³ uses the cone formula (one-third); 36,960 cm³ uses the diameter 28 cm as the radius; 19,800 cm³ multiplies the curved surface area by the height.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A hollow metal sphere has an external radius of 6 cm and an internal radius of 4 cm. It is melted and recast into a solid cylinder of base radius 4 cm. What is the height of the cylinder?

solution.concept: Volume of metal in a hollow sphere = 4/3 π (R³ − r³); equate it to πr²h (π cancels)
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 cm uses the whole outer sphere (ignores the hollow); 5⅓ cm uses only the inner sphere; 9.5 cm forgets the 4/3 in the sphere's volume (152/16).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two fair coins are tossed together. What is the probability of getting at most one head?

solution.concept: List the 4 equally likely outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT
solution.explanation: At most one head means 0 or 1 head: HT, TH and TT — 3 of the 4 outcomes. Probability = 3/4.
steps: At most one head: HT, TH, TT
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/4 is the probability of two heads; 1/2 counts only exactly one head; 2/3 treats 'no head, one head, two heads' as three equally likely outcomes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability that the number shown is greater than 4 or is even?

solution.concept: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); here count the favourable faces directly
solution.explanation: Greater than 4: 5, 6. Even: 2, 4, 6. Together: 2, 4, 5, 6 — 4 faces. Probability = 4/6 = 2/3.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5/6 adds 2/6 and 3/6 without removing the 6 counted twice; 1/2 counts only the even numbers; 1/3 counts only the numbers greater than 4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bag contains 6 white and 4 black balls. Two balls are drawn at random together. What is the probability that both are white?

solution.concept: P = (ways to choose 2 white) ÷ (ways to choose any 2) = ⁶C₂ ÷ ¹⁰C₂
solution.explanation: ⁶C₂ = 15 and ¹⁰C₂ = 45, so the probability is 15/45 = 1/3.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9/25 draws with replacement (6/10 × 6/10); 3/5 is the chance for one white ball only; 2/15 is the probability that both are black.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: One card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that it is neither a heart nor a king?

solution.concept: Count hearts or kings without double-counting the king of hearts, then take the complement
solution.explanation: Hearts = 13 and kings = 4, but the king of hearts is in both, so 16 cards are a heart or a king. The rest, 36 cards, are neither: 36/52 = 9/13.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3/4 removes only the hearts; 35/52 removes 13 + 4 = 17 cards, counting the king of hearts twice; 12/13 removes only the kings.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A family has three children. Assuming each child is equally likely to be a boy or a girl, independently of the others, what is the probability that the family has at least one boy and at least one girl?

solution.concept: The complement of 'at least one of each' is 'all boys or all girls'
solution.explanation: There are 2³ = 8 equally likely outcomes. Only BBB and GGG fail, so the probability is 1 − 2/8 = 3/4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7/8 is the probability of at least one boy only; 3/8 is the probability of exactly two boys; 1/2 assumes the two kinds of mixed family are the only outcomes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A box contains 20 balls numbered 1 to 20. Two balls are drawn at random together. What is the probability that the sum of their numbers is even?

solution.concept: An even sum needs two even numbers or two odd numbers
solution.explanation: There are 10 odd and 10 even numbers. Both even: ¹⁰C₂ = 45; both odd: 45. Favourable = 90 out of ²⁰C₂ = 190, so P = 90/190 = 9/19.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/2 treats the two draws as independent (with replacement); 9/38 counts only the both-even case; 10/19 is the probability of an odd sum.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B take turns to throw a fair die, A throwing first. The first person to throw a six wins. What is the probability that A wins?

solution.concept: A wins on throw 1, 3, 5, …: add a geometric series with ratio (5/6)²
steps: Each later chance needs two misses first: × 25/36
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/2 ignores A's advantage of throwing first; 1/6 counts only A's first throw; 5/11 is B's probability of winning.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many ways can a captain and a vice-captain be chosen from a team of 11 players?

solution.concept: Order matters (the two posts are different): ¹¹P₂ = 11 × 10
solution.explanation: The captain can be any of 11 players and the vice-captain any of the remaining 10, so there are 11 × 10 = 110 ways.
solution.why_others_wrong: 55 = ¹¹C₂ ignores that the two posts are different; 121 lets the same player hold both posts; 22 adds 11 + 11 instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many different arrangements of the letters of the word ACCOUNT begin with A and end with T?

solution.concept: Fix the end letters; arrange the middle letters, dividing by the factorial of any repeated letter
solution.explanation: With A first and T last, the middle five letters are C, C, O, U, N, with C repeated. Arrangements = 5!/2! = 120/2 = 60.
steps: Middle: C, C, O, U, N
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 forgets that the two C's are identical; 2,520 = 7!/2! counts all arrangements of ACCOUNT; 30 divides by 2 twice.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many three-digit numbers have their digits in strictly increasing order from left to right (for example 147)?

solution.concept: Any 3 different non-zero digits can be written in increasing order in exactly one way
solution.explanation: 0 cannot appear: it cannot be the first digit and cannot follow a larger digit. So choose any 3 of the digits 1–9: ⁹C₃ = 84, and each choice gives exactly one number.
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 = ¹⁰C₃ wrongly allows the digit 0; 504 = 9 × 8 × 7 counts every order of three different digits; 165 = ¹¹C₃ counts digits that may repeat (non-decreasing).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the total value of the payments received by fuel merchants in the week?

solution.concept: Total value = number of payments × average value
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,62,000 drops a zero; ₹19,20,000 is the electronics total; ₹2,700 adds the two figures instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which category received the largest total value of payments in the week?

solution.concept: Compare number × average value for every row, not either column alone
