solution.explanation: Totals: Grocery ₹8.4 lakh, Pharmacy ₹7.2 lakh, Fuel ₹16.2 lakh, Restaurants ₹8.4 lakh, Electronics 300 × 6,400 = ₹19.2 lakh. Electronics is the largest despite having the fewest payments.
solution.why_others_wrong: Fuel is second (₹16.2 lakh); Grocery has the most payments but a small average value; Restaurants total only ₹8.4 lakh.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average value of a payment across all five categories taken together?

solution.concept: Overall average = total value ÷ total number of payments (a weighted average)
solution.explanation: Total value = ₹59,40,000 and total payments = 7,200, so the average = 59,40,000 ÷ 7,200 = ₹825.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,766 is the simple average of the five averages, which ignores how many payments each has; ₹11,88,000 is the average value per category; ₹82.50 slips a decimal place.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In the next week, the number of restaurant payments rises by 25% and their average value falls by 8%; the other four categories do not change. By what percentage does the total value of all payments increase (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: A change in one row moves the total by (change in that row) ÷ (old total)
solution.why_others_wrong: 15% is the change in the restaurants' own value (1.25 × 0.92 = 1.15); 2.4% adds the rates (+17%) instead of multiplying them before weighting; 2.5% weights the 15% by the restaurants' share of payments (1/6) instead of their share of value.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many individual policies did Rohan sell?

solution.concept: Individual policies = policies sold × (100 − family-floater %)
solution.explanation: Rohan sold 260 policies, 45% of them family floaters (117). The remaining 55% = 143 were individual policies.
solution.why_others_wrong: 117 is Rohan's family-floater count; 260 is all the policies he sold; 156 is Kavya's individual policies.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the total annual premium on the policies sold by Imran?

solution.concept: Price each kind of policy separately and add
solution.explanation: Imran: 20% of 300 = 60 family floaters × ₹30,000 = ₹18,00,000, and 240 individual policies × ₹12,000 = ₹28,80,000. Total = ₹46,80,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹36,00,000 prices all 300 policies at ₹12,000; ₹63,00,000 uses the average of the two premiums for every policy; ₹28,80,000 counts only the individual policies.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Each agent earns a commission of 15% of the premium on family-floater policies and 10% of the premium on individual policies. Which agent earned the lowest commission?

solution.concept: Commission per family floater = ₹4,500; per individual policy = ₹1,200
solution.why_others_wrong: Sujata sold the fewest policies, but 60% of them were high-commission floaters (₹5,72,400); Kavya is close but higher at ₹5,65,200; Rohan earned the most.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which year did the office issue exactly twice as many passports as in 2021?

solution.concept: Double the 2021 bar and look for a matching bar
solution.explanation: In 2021 the office issued 36 thousand passports. Twice that is 72 thousand, which is the figure for 2022.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2023 (90 thousand) is 2.5 times 2021; 2024 (81 thousand) is 2.25 times; 2025 (99 thousand) is 2.75 times.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the median of the yearly numbers of passports issued from 2020 to 2025?

solution.concept: Median of an even number of values = average of the two middle values after sorting
solution.explanation: Sorted (thousand): 36, 48, 72, 81, 90, 99. The two middle values are 72 and 81, so the median = (72 + 81) ÷ 2 = 76.5 thousand = 76,500.
solution.why_others_wrong: 71,000 is the mean, not the median; 81,000 takes only the fourth sorted value; 85,500 averages the middle two years (2023 and 2024) without sorting.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many years from 2021 to 2025 did the number of passports issued change (rise or fall) by more than 20% compared with the previous year?

solution.concept: Percentage change = change ÷ previous year's figure; count falls as well as rises
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 counts only the rises and misses the 25% fall in 2021; 5 includes 2024 (only −10%); 2 divides each change by the later year's figure instead of the previous year's.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In 2025, 12% of the passports issued were Tatkaal passports with a fee of ₹3,500 each, and the rest were normal passports with a fee of ₹1,500 each. What was the total fee collected on the passports issued in 2025?

solution.concept: Split the year's total by type, price each part, then add
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹14,85,00,000 charges every passport the normal fee; ₹34,65,00,000 charges every passport the Tatkaal fee; ₹24,75,00,000 uses the simple average fee of ₹2,500.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: At which mandi was the difference between the paddy procured and the wheat procured the smallest?

solution.concept: Read the two bars of each mandi and subtract the smaller from the larger
solution.explanation: Differences (thousand tonnes): P 42 − 30 = 12, Q 45 − 36 = 9, R 52 − 28 = 24, S 54 − 33 = 21. The smallest is at Mandi Q.
solution.why_others_wrong: Mandi P has the next smallest gap (12); Mandi R has the largest gap (24); Mandi S's gap is 21.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Assume the agencies paid ₹2,300 per quintal for paddy and ₹2,400 per quintal for wheat (1 tonne = 10 quintals). What was the total value of the paddy and wheat procured at Mandi Q?

solution.concept: Convert thousand tonnes to quintals, then price each crop separately
solution.explanation: Paddy: 36,000 t = 3,60,000 quintals × ₹2,300 = ₹82.8 crore. Wheat: 45,000 t = 4,50,000 quintals × ₹2,400 = ₹108 crore. Total = ₹190.8 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹19.08 crore forgets that 1 tonne is 10 quintals; ₹189.9 crore swaps the two prices; ₹190.35 crore prices all 81,000 tonnes at the average ₹2,350.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average paddy procurement of the mandis at which wheat procurement exceeded 40 thousand tonnes?

solution.concept: First pick the mandis using the wheat bars, then average their paddy bars
solution.explanation: Wheat exceeded 40 thousand tonnes only at Q (45) and R (52). Their paddy figures are 36 and 28, whose average is 32 thousand tonnes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 is the average paddy of all four mandis; 48.5 averages the wheat figures of Q and R; 48 averages the paddy of the other two mandis (P and S).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much did the households save in mutual funds in 2025-26?

solution.concept: Amount = share % × total
solution.explanation: Mutual funds: 18% of ₹2,400 crore = ₹432 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹360 crore is the small-savings figure (15%); ₹43.2 crore slips a decimal place; ₹336 crore is gold (14%).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: For how many of the six instruments did the households save more than ₹300 crore?

solution.concept: ₹300 crore is 12.5% of ₹2,400 crore, so count the shares above 12.5%
solution.explanation: ₹300 crore ÷ ₹2,400 crore = 12.5%. Shares above 12.5%: bank deposits (35%), small savings (15%), mutual funds (18%) and gold (14%). Insurance (12% = ₹288 crore) and others (6%) fall short. So 4 instruments.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 misses gold (14% = ₹336 crore); 5 includes insurance (₹288 crore); 2 counts only the shares above 15%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The district has 6 lakh households. What was the average saving per household in bank deposits in 2025-26?

solution.concept: 1 crore = 100 lakh; divide the bank-deposit amount by the number of households
solution.explanation: Bank deposits = 35% of ₹2,400 crore = ₹840 crore = ₹8,40,00,00,000. Dividing by 6,00,000 households gives ₹14,000 per household.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹40,000 divides all savings (₹2,400 crore) by the households; ₹1,400 and ₹1,40,000 slip a place in the crore-to-lakh conversion.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In 2025-26 the instruments earned these annual returns: bank deposits 6.5%, small savings 7.5%, mutual funds 12%, insurance 5%, gold 10% and others 4%. What total return did the district's savings earn in the year?

solution.concept: Total return = Σ (amount in each instrument × its rate); the overall rate is a weighted average
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹180 crore uses the simple average of the six rates (7.5%); ₹156 crore applies the bank-deposit rate to everything; ₹18.72 crore slips a decimal place.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The gold savings were split between physical gold and gold ETFs in the ratio 5 : 2, and the insurance savings between life and health insurance in the ratio 3 : 1. What is the ratio of the savings in physical gold to the savings in health insurance?

solution.concept: Find each sector's amount first, then apply the inner ratio within that sector
solution.explanation: Gold = ₹336 crore, so physical gold = 5/7 × 336 = ₹240 crore. Insurance = ₹288 crore, so health = 1/4 × 288 = ₹72 crore. Ratio = 240 : 72 = 10 : 3.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 : 6 compares all gold with all insurance; 5 : 1 compares the ratio terms without the sector sizes; 10 : 9 uses life insurance (₹216 crore) instead of health insurance.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What were the total deposits held in the bank's savings accounts in Satara?

solution.concept: Use the deposits pie for money and the accounts pie for numbers of accounts
solution.explanation: Satara's share of deposits is 25%, so its deposits are 25% of ₹1,200 crore = ₹300 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹360 crore uses Satara's share of accounts (30%) instead of deposits; ₹30 crore slips a decimal place; ₹250 crore takes 25% of ₹1,000 crore.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average deposit per savings account in Raigad?

solution.concept: Average deposit = district's deposits ÷ district's accounts; take each from its own pie
solution.explanation: Raigad: deposits = 30% of ₹1,200 crore = ₹360 crore; accounts = 25% of 2,40,000 = 60,000. Average = ₹360 crore ÷ 60,000 = ₹60,000.
solution.shortcut: Average = overall average (₹50,000) × deposit share ÷ account share = 50,000 × 30/25.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹50,000 is the bank-wide average; ₹6,000 slips a place in converting crore; ₹41,666.67 is Satara's average.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many of the five districts was the average deposit per account higher than the bank's overall average deposit per account?

solution.concept: A district's average beats the overall average exactly when its share of deposits exceeds its share of accounts
solution.explanation: Overall average = ₹1,200 crore ÷ 2,40,000 = ₹50,000. Compare the shares: Raigad 30% > 25% ✓, Ratnagiri 15% < 20%, Sindhudurg 11% > 10% ✓, Satara 25% < 30%, Sangli 19% > 15% ✓. So 3 districts.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 misses Sindhudurg, whose shares (11% vs 10%) are close; 4 includes Satara, which has the most accounts but a smaller deposit share; 1 counts only Raigad, the largest deposit share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Next year Ratnagiri's number of accounts grows by 25% and its deposits grow by 40%. What will be its average deposit per account?

solution.concept: New average = old average × (1 + deposit growth) ÷ (1 + account growth)
solution.explanation: Now: deposits ₹180 crore, accounts 48,000, average ₹37,500. Next year: deposits ₹252 crore, accounts 60,000, average = ₹252 crore ÷ 60,000 = ₹42,000 (= 37,500 × 1.4 ÷ 1.25).
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹52,500 applies the 40% deposit growth but ignores the new accounts; ₹43,125 adds the net 15% (40 − 25) to the average; ₹33,482.14 inverts the two growth factors.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By how many rupees per quintal did the price rise from March to June?

solution.concept: Read the two points and subtract
solution.explanation: March: ₹1,350; June: ₹2,430. Rise = ₹1,080 per quintal.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹405 is the rise from May to June only; ₹630 is the rise from January to June; ₹270 is the rise from March to April.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many of the six months was the price higher than its six-month average?

solution.concept: Average = sum of the six prices ÷ 6; then compare each month
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 misses January, which is only ₹12.50 above the average; 4 adds April (₹1,620); 1 counts only June.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A restaurant spends exactly ₹24,300 on onions every month at the month's wholesale price. How many more kilograms of onions did it get in March than in June?

solution.concept: Quantity = money spent ÷ price; convert quintals to kg
solution.explanation: March: 24,300 ÷ 1,350 = 18 quintals = 1,800 kg. June: 24,300 ÷ 2,430 = 10 quintals = 1,000 kg. Difference = 800 kg.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,800 kg is the March quantity alone; 8 kg forgets that 1 quintal is 100 kg; 600 kg compares March with May (1,200 kg) instead of June.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader bought 40 quintals of onions in February at February's price and sold them in May at May's price. 5% of the onions (by weight) were lost in storage. What was his profit percentage (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Revenue comes only from the quantity left after the loss; profit % is on the purchase cost
solution.why_others_wrong: 35% ignores the storage loss (price rise from ₹1,500 to ₹2,025); 30% subtracts 5 from 35 instead of applying the loss to the quantity; 22.03% divides the profit by the revenue instead of the cost.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many of the South depot's buses are on the road on a working day?

solution.concept: South's fleet = 2/10 of 300; take 85% of it
solution.explanation: South has 2/10 × 300 = 60 buses, and 85% of 60 = 51 are on the road.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 is South's whole fleet; 9 is the number under maintenance; 54 uses North's 90% instead of South's 85%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the total distance run by all the buses on the road on a working day?

solution.concept: Distance = buses on the road × km per bus, depot by depot
solution.why_others_wrong: 59,400 km counts the buses under maintenance as well; 51,600 km gives all 258 buses on the road 200 km each; 53,320 km uses the simple average of the three daily runs for every bus.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the North depot's daily diesel bill?

solution.concept: Diesel used = km ÷ 4; cost = litres × ₹90
solution.explanation: North's buses on the road run 24,300 km, using 24,300 ÷ 4 = 6,075 litres. Cost = 6,075 × 90 = ₹5,46,750.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹6,07,500 includes the 15 buses under maintenance; ₹21,87,000 multiplies the km (not the litres) by ₹90; ₹2,75,400 is the South depot's bill.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage is the energy cost per km of an electric bus lower than the fuel cost per km of a diesel bus (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Cost per km: diesel = ₹90 ÷ 4 km; electric = 1.2 kWh × ₹8. 'Lower than diesel' uses the diesel cost as the base
solution.explanation: Diesel: ₹22.50 per km. Electric: ₹9.60 per km. The electric bus is ₹12.90 cheaper, which is 12.90 ÷ 22.50 = 57.33% lower.
solution.why_others_wrong: 134.38% divides the saving by the electric cost (how much more diesel costs); 42.67% is the electric cost as a percentage of the diesel cost; 12.9% reads the ₹12.90 saving as a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the undertaking's 300 buses are under maintenance on a working day?

solution.concept: Count the buses off the road at each depot, then divide by the whole fleet
solution.explanation: Off the road: North 15, Central 18, South 9 — 42 buses. 42 ÷ 300 = 14%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15% is the simple average of 10%, 20% and 15%, which ignores the different fleet sizes; 86% is the share on the road; 16.28% divides by the 258 buses on the road instead of the whole fleet.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The undertaking replaces all of North's diesel buses with electric buses like Central's, keeping the same number on the road and the same daily km per bus. How much will it save on North's daily energy bill?

solution.concept: Saving = North's daily km × (diesel cost per km − electric cost per km)
solution.explanation: North runs 24,300 km a day. Saving per km = 22.50 − 9.60 = ₹12.90. Daily saving = 24,300 × 12.90 = ₹3,13,470 (diesel bill ₹5,46,750 minus electricity bill ₹2,33,280).
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹5,46,750 is the whole diesel bill, as if electricity were free; ₹2,33,280 is the new electricity bill; ₹3,48,300 counts all 150 North buses, including those under maintenance.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much grain does the shop distribute to PHH cards in a month?

solution.concept: PHH grain = 5 kg × total members on PHH cards
solution.why_others_wrong: 4,500 kg gives 5 kg per card instead of per member; 18,000 kg assumes 4 members on every card; 31,500 kg gives every PHH card the AAY quota of 35 kg.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much rice in all does the shop distribute in a month?

solution.concept: Total grain = AAY + PHH; rice is 3/5 of it
solution.why_others_wrong: 10,860 kg is the wheat; 9,990 kg is the rice for PHH cards only; 16,650 kg is the PHH grain, not the rice.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the grain given to PHH cards goes to cards with 4 or more members (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: PHH grain is proportional to members, not to cards
solution.explanation: Members on cards with 4, 5 or 6 members: 1,200 + 750 + 360 = 2,310 out of 3,330. Share = 2,310 ÷ 3,330 = 69.37%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 56.67% uses the share of cards (510 of 900) instead of members; 30.63% is the share of the smaller families; 36.04% counts only the 4-member cards.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What commission does the shopkeeper earn in a month?

solution.concept: Commission = ₹1.50 × all grain distributed (AAY + PHH)
solution.explanation: Total grain = 27,150 kg, so the commission = 27,150 × 1.50 = ₹40,725.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹24,975 counts only PHH grain; ₹15,750 counts only AAY grain; ₹4,07,250 slips a decimal place.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Next month, 50 of the 6-member PHH cards are converted into AAY cards, and 100 new 3-member PHH cards are issued. How does the shop's total monthly grain distribution change?

solution.concept: Track each change: a converted card stops getting 5 kg × 6 and starts getting 35 kg
solution.explanation: Each converted card changes from 30 kg (PHH) to 35 kg (AAY): +5 kg × 50 = +250 kg. The new cards add 100 × 15 = 1,500 kg. Net change = +1,750 kg.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3,250 kg adds the AAY quota of the converted cards without removing their old PHH quota; 250 kg forgets the new cards; 1,500 kg forgets the conversion.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the utilisation of ATM-1?

solution.concept: Utilisation = cash withdrawn ÷ cash loaded × 100
solution.explanation: ATM-1: ₹30 lakh withdrawn out of ₹40 lakh loaded = 75%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 133.33% divides the other way; 25% is the share left unused; 10% reads the ₹10 lakh left as a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much cash was loaded into ATM-5?

solution.concept: Cash loaded = cash withdrawn ÷ utilisation
solution.explanation: ₹28 lakh was 70% of the cash loaded, so the cash loaded = 28 ÷ 0.7 = ₹40 lakh.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹19.6 lakh takes 70% of 28; ₹36.4 lakh adds 30% to 28; ₹12 lakh is the cash left unused.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many withdrawals were made at ATM-2?

solution.concept: Number of withdrawals = cash withdrawn ÷ average withdrawal (convert lakh to rupees)
solution.explanation: ATM-2: ₹36 lakh = ₹36,00,000 withdrawn at an average of ₹2,400, so 36,00,000 ÷ 2,400 = 1,500 withdrawals.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15,000 and 150 slip a place in the lakh conversion; 1,875 divides the cash loaded (₹45 lakh) instead of the cash withdrawn.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which ATM had the highest average amount per withdrawal?

solution.concept: Fill the missing averages: average = cash withdrawn ÷ number of withdrawals

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The least common multiple (LCM) of 12, 18 and 30
Quantity II: The square of the prime number 13

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: LCM: take the highest power of each prime
solution.explanation: 12 = 2² × 3, 18 = 2 × 3², 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, so the LCM = 2² × 3² × 5 = 180. 13² = 169. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' and '≤' come from taking the HCF (6) or a smaller common multiple such as 90 instead of the LCM.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The number of seconds in 2.5 hours
Quantity II: The number of minutes in 6.5 days

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Convert units step by step: 1 hour = 3,600 s; 1 day = 1,440 min
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 2.5 × 3,600 = 9,000. Quantity II = 6.5 × 1,440 = 9,360. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' and '≥' come from taking a day as 20 hours or 6.5 days as 6 days 5 hours (6 × 1,440 + 300 = 8,940).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Selling price (₹) of an article marked ₹1,040 and sold at a 7% discount
Quantity II: Selling price (₹) of an article that costs ₹840 and is sold at a 15% profit

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Discount: SP = MP × (1 − d%); profit: SP = CP × (1 + p%)
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 1,040 × 0.93 = ₹967.20. Quantity II = 840 × 1.15 = ₹966. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' and '≤' come from judging by the percentages alone (a 15% profit looks larger than a 7% cut) without working out the two prices.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The number of hours in 4 weeks
Quantity II: The sum of the interior angles of a hexagon (in degrees)

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Sum of interior angles of an n-sided polygon = (n − 2) × 180°
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 4 × 7 × 24 = 672. Quantity II = (6 − 2) × 180 = 720. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' and '≥' come from taking the hexagon's angle sum as 6 × 90° = 540° or as 360°.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Days 7 workers take to finish a job that 4 workers finish in 50 days (all work at the same rate)
Quantity II: Minutes a tap pouring 15 litres per minute takes to fill a 420-litre tank

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Workers × days is constant for a fixed job; time = capacity ÷ rate
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 4 × 50 ÷ 7 = 200/7 ≈ 28.57 days. Quantity II = 420 ÷ 15 = 28 minutes. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' and '≤' come from rounding 200/7 down to 28 or below, or from taking 420 ÷ 15 as 30.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The value of x, where x² − 5x − 14 = 0
Quantity II: The value of y, where y² − 17y + 72 = 0

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Find every root; compare the largest value of Quantity I with the smallest of Quantity II
solution.explanation: I: (x − 7)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 7 or −2. II: (y − 8)(y − 9) = 0, so y = 8 or 9. The largest x (7) is below the smallest y (8), so Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' and '≥' come from taking the roots of II with the wrong sign (−8 and −9).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Volume (cm³) of a cylinder of radius 3.5 cm and height 9 cm (take π = 22/7)
Quantity II: Volume (cm³) of a cube of edge 7 cm

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Cylinder: V = πr²h; cube: V = a³
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 22/7 × 12.25 × 9 = 38.5 × 9 = 346.5 cm³. Quantity II = 7³ = 343 cm³. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' and '≤' come from using π = 3, which gives 3 × 12.25 × 9 = 330.75 cm³.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The number of arrangements of the letters of the word BANK
Quantity II: The number of ways of choosing 2 people from 7

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Arrangements of n different letters = n!; selections = ⁿCᵣ
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 4! = 24 (all four letters are different). Quantity II = ⁷C₂ = 21. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' and '≤' come from using ⁷P₂ = 42 for the selection, where order does not matter.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The probability that a leap year chosen at random has 53 Sundays
Quantity II: The probability of getting exactly two heads when three fair coins are tossed

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A leap year has 52 full weeks and 2 extra days; count the favourable outcomes for the coins
solution.explanation: Quantity I: the 2 extra days are one of 7 equally likely pairs (Sun–Mon, Mon–Tue, …, Sat–Sun); 2 of them contain a Sunday, so P = 2/7 ≈ 0.286. Quantity II: HHT, HTH, THH — 3 of 8 outcomes, P = 0.375. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' and '≥' come from counting only one two-head arrangement (HHT), which gives 1/8 for Quantity II.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Average speed (km/h) of a car that covers 80 km in 3 hours 45 minutes
Quantity II: A's present age (years), if A is now twice as old as B and in 10 years A will be 1.5 times as old as B

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Convert 3 h 45 min to 3.75 h; set up the age equations with B as the unknown
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 80 ÷ 3.75 = 21⅓ km/h. Quantity II: A = 2B and 2B + 10 = 1.5(B + 10), so 0.5B = 5, B = 10 and A = 20. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' and '≤' come from giving A's age 10 years from now (30) instead of his present age.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The value of x, where 2x² − 9x + 4 = 0
Quantity II: The value of y, where 3y² − 7y + 2 = 0

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: When the roots interleave, no single relation holds for every pair
solution.explanation: I: (2x − 1)(x − 4) = 0, so x = 4 or 1/2. II: (3y − 1)(y − 2) = 0, so y = 1/3 or 2. x = 4 is above both y values, but x = 1/2 lies between them (above 1/3, below 2). So the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' uses only x = 4; '≤' and '<' use only x = 1/2 against y = 2.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the cost of fencing a square field all round?
I. The area of the field is 2,500 m².
II. Fencing costs ₹25 per metre.

options.text: Both statements I and II together are needed
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Statements I and II together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Cost of fencing = perimeter × rate; the perimeter needs the side, the cost needs the rate
solution.explanation: I gives the side (√2,500 = 50 m) and so the perimeter (200 m), but not the rate. II gives the rate but not the size. Together: 200 × 25 = ₹5,000.
steps: I alone: perimeter 200 m, rate unknown
II alone: rate known, size unknown
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' forgets that the rate is needed; 'II alone' forgets that the size is needed; 'not sufficient even together' misses that the two combine directly.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both statements I and II together are needed

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the volume of the cube?
I. The total surface area of the cube is 294 cm².
II. The diagonal of one face of the cube is 7√2 cm.

options.text: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Both statements I and II together are needed

solution.concept: Any one measurement of a cube fixes its edge, and hence its volume
solution.explanation: I: 6a² = 294 ⇒ a² = 49 ⇒ a = 7 cm, volume 343 cm³ — sufficient. II: face diagonal = a√2 = 7√2 ⇒ a = 7 cm — sufficient. Either statement alone answers the question.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' or 'II alone' overlooks that the other statement also fixes the edge; 'both together' assumes the two must be combined.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: How many marks did Ravi score in Mathematics?
I. His total in Mathematics, Science and English is 225.
II. His average in Science and English is 70.
III. His Mathematics marks are 15 more than his Science marks.

options.text: Any two of the three statements together are sufficient
Only I and II together are sufficient
Only I and III together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary

solution.concept: Check every pair: a pair is sufficient only if it fixes the Mathematics marks
solution.explanation: I + II: Science + English = 140, so Mathematics = 225 − 140 = 85 — sufficient. I + III: M + S + E = 225 and M = S + 15 leave E free — not sufficient. II + III: S + E = 140 and M = S + 15 leave S free — not sufficient. No statement works alone.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Any two' assumes every pair works, but I + III and II + III each leave a subject's marks free; 'only I and III' misses that English is still unknown; 'all three' is more than needed.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only I and II together are sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the value of the positive integer n?
I. n² − 13n + 36 = 0
II. n is a factor of 36 and a perfect square greater than 1.

options.text: Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are needed
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

solution.concept: List every value each statement allows; a set of statements is sufficient only if exactly one value survives
solution.explanation: I: (n − 4)(n − 9) = 0 ⇒ n = 4 or 9. II: perfect-square factors of 36 greater than 1 are 4, 9 and 36. Together n can still be 4 or 9, so even both statements together are not sufficient.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Both together' assumes the overlap is a single value, but both 4 and 9 satisfy I and II; 'I alone' and 'either' forget that a quadratic gives two positive roots here.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statements I and II together are not sufficient
